title: Meet the OS
about: What the operating system manages, ending frozen apps, and safe updates.

cards.prompt: Your music is playing, a game wants its sound effects, and a message has just arrived with a ping. All three apps want the **speaker**, right now.

choices.text: The app that grabbed the speaker first keeps it until it closes
choices.consequence: Then the music would hog the speaker, and you'd never hear the ping. Apps can't just grab shared things and keep them.

choices.text: Each app drives the speaker itself, whenever it likes
choices.consequence: Three apps all driving one speaker at once would crash into each other. Something has to share it out.

choices.text: One main program shares it out, so you hear all three
choices.consequence: Yes. The ping plays over the music, and the game's sounds too. Every app gets heard.

cards.explanation: Apps share the [[CPU]], [[RAM]], the screen and the speaker. If each one grabbed what it wanted, they'd crash into each other. So one main program is in charge of sharing: the **operating system**.
cards.hint: Think of a referee in a game. Should players grab the ball and keep it, or should someone share out turns?

cards.title: The operating system
cards.body:
That main program is the **operating system**, or **OS**. It's the referee:

- It gives each app quick turns on the [[CPU]], so they all seem to run at once.
- It shares out [[RAM]] and stops apps reading each other's data.
- It talks to the **hardware** (screen, keyboard, speaker, Wi-Fi), so apps don't have to.

cards.prompt: Whose job is it: the **operating system's**, or an **app's**?

items.label: Decide which app uses the CPU next
Share out RAM between open apps
Talk to the keyboard, screen and Wi-Fi
Stop apps reading each other's data
Add a funny filter to a selfie

cards.explanation: The **OS** manages the shared things every app needs: CPU time, RAM, the hardware and safety. **Apps** do one particular job for you, and ask the OS for what they need.
cards.hint: Think of the OS as the referee. Is this job about sharing something every app needs, or one particular thing an app does for you?
cards.nudge: The OS handles the shared things: CPU turns, RAM, [[hardware]] and keeping apps apart. Apps do one particular job for you.

cards.prompt: Your laptop has frozen. This is its **task manager**: it lists every running program (each one is a **process**) and how much of the [[CPU]] it's using. **System** is the OS itself: end it and the laptop crashes. End whatever is hogging the CPU, but **keep your music and your [[browser]] open**.
cards.explanation: The **drawing app** was stuck using 85% of the CPU. Ending its process freed the CPU, and everything else carried on. You'd lose anything unsaved in the drawing app, but nothing else. Ending **System** would have crashed the whole laptop.
cards.hint: Look at the CPU number for each process. Which one is taking far more than the rest?
cards.nudge: End only the process hogging the CPU. Never end **System**, and keep your music and browser running.

cards.prompt: This laptop gets slower the longer it's on. One app keeps grabbing [[RAM]] and never gives it back (a **memory leak**). Move time forward to **40 minutes or more**, find that app and end it. Keep the music on.
cards.explanation: The **chat app** grew by 0.15 GB every minute. After 40 minutes it was using 6.5 GB and filled the 8 GB of RAM almost on its own. Ending it gives the memory back. Restarting the app (or the laptop) is the everyday fix for a leak, until the app's makers fix it.
cards.hint: Slide time forward first, then watch the RAM each app uses. Which one keeps growing when the others stay the same?
cards.nudge: A leaky app's RAM keeps climbing over time. Move time to 40 minutes or more, and don't end the music or **System**.

cards.prompt: You're halfway through an essay on your laptop. **Updates** are new versions of the OS. They fix **bugs** (mistakes in a program) and close **security holes** (weak spots attackers could use).

steps.text: A message pops up: **"Updates are ready. Restart now?"**

choices.consequence: The unsaved essay was only in [[RAM]]. Restarting cleared it, and your work is gone.

choices.text: Save the essay first, then restart
choices.consequence: The essay is safe in [[storage]], and the update can start.
Then the security holes stay open, and attackers know about them. Your laptop gets less safe over time.

steps.text: The screen says **"Working on updates. Don't turn off your device."** It's been ten minutes.

choices.text: Hold the power button to stop it
choices.consequence: Cutting an update off halfway can leave the OS broken and unable to start.

choices.text: Plug in the charger and let it finish
choices.consequence: Big updates can take a while. Keeping it powered lets it finish safely.

cards.explanation: **Save your work**, then let updates install. Keep the device plugged in, and never switch it off halfway: that can leave the OS broken. Updates fix bugs and close security holes.
cards.hint: Think about where unsaved work lives, and what happens to it when a device restarts. Then think about what switching off halfway would do.

cards.prompt: You're browsing, and the screen suddenly flashes red. Good to know: a web page can't see what's on your laptop.

steps.text: **"WARNING! Your laptop has 5 [[viruses|virus]]! Download CleanerPro now or call this number!"**

choices.consequence: Pop-ups like this are fakes. The "cleaner" is usually the harmful program itself.
It's a scam. The caller will ask for money or for control of your laptop.

choices.text: Don't click anything in it. Close the tab
choices.consequence: A web page knowing what's on your laptop is like a billboard knowing what's in your fridge. This warning is fake.

steps.text: The page keeps popping back up and the tab won't close.

choices.text: End the browser in the task manager, then tell a parent or teacher
choices.consequence: The page is gone, and they can help you check everything is fine.
Buttons on a fake pop-up can do anything, including start a download.

cards.explanation: A web page can't see what's on your laptop, so a pop-up claiming to have found viruses is **fake**. Don't click anything inside it. Close the browser (with the task manager if you need to) and tell a parent, teacher or someone you trust.
cards.hint: Can a web page really see what's on your laptop? Think about who can, and whether you should click anything it shows you.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The **OS** is the referee: it shares out CPU, RAM and hardware.
- Frozen app? End its process in the task manager, never System.
- Save your work, then let updates finish.

Next: where your files actually live.
